title: TypeScript and React
description: JavaScript runtime, TypeScript types, React rendering and hooks, tooling and web basics.

cards.question: Same script, promise already resolved: which runs first, `.then(cb)` or `setTimeout(cb, 0)`?
cards.explanation: Promise callbacks are microtasks, which run before the event loop takes the next task, such as a timer.

cards.question: `NaN === NaN` is true in JavaScript.
cards.explanation: NaN is not equal to anything, including itself. Use `Number.isNaN(x)` to test for it.

cards.question: What does `[] === []` evaluate to?
cards.explanation: Objects and arrays compare by reference. Two separate empty arrays are different objects, so strict equality is false.

cards.question: What does `Promise.all` do if one of its promises rejects?
cards.explanation: `Promise.all` fails fast. Use `Promise.allSettled` when you need every result, whether fulfilled or rejected.

cards.question: `items.forEach(async x => await save(x))` waits for every save before the next line runs.
cards.explanation: forEach ignores the promises its callback returns. Use `for...of` with await for sequential work, or `await Promise.all(items.map(save))`.

cards.question: What is the key difference between `unknown` and `any`?
options: They are aliases for the same type
cards.explanation: Both accept any value, but `any` turns off checking. `unknown` makes you narrow it first, so it is the safe type for untrusted data.

cards.question: TypeScript types are erased at compile time and don't exist at runtime.
cards.explanation: So a type annotation or `as User` can't validate data from an API. Use runtime checks or a schema library for that.

cards.question: Two TypeScript types with the same shape are compatible even if they have different names.
cards.explanation: TypeScript is structurally typed: compatibility depends on members, not on declared names.

cards.question: For `x: string | number`, which check narrows `x` to `string`?
cards.explanation: `typeof` checks the primitive type at runtime, and TypeScript narrows on it. `as` only asserts and checks nothing.

cards.question: What does the generic in `function first<T>(xs: T[]): T` give callers?
options: A return type that matches the items
cards.explanation: T is inferred from the argument, so `first([1, 2])` returns number and `first(["a"])` returns string, with full type checking.

cards.question: Why does React want a stable `key` on each list item?
options: To match items to their state across renders
cards.explanation: Keys tell React which item is which between renders, so state and DOM nodes stay with the right item when the list changes.

cards.question: Using the array index as `key` is safe when list items can be reordered or removed.
cards.explanation: When items move, index keys attach the wrong state and DOM to the wrong item. Use a stable id from the data instead.

cards.question: Why might `items.push(x); setItems(items)` not re-render?
options: Same array reference, so React sees no change
Arrays can't be stored in state
cards.explanation: React compares state with Object.is. Create a new array, like `setItems([...items, x])`, so the change is detected.

cards.question: By default, when a component re-renders, its child components re-render too.
cards.explanation: Children re-render with their parent unless they are wrapped in `memo` and their props are unchanged.

cards.question: Right after `setCount(count + 1)`, what does `count` hold in the same handler?
options: A promise of the new value
The old value until the next render
cards.explanation: State is a snapshot per render. Setting it schedules a new render; use `setCount(c => c + 1)` when the update depends on the previous value.

cards.question: When does a `useEffect` cleanup function run?
options: Before the effect re-runs and on unmount
After every state change in the app
cards.explanation: Cleanup undoes the previous effect, such as removing a listener, before the next run with new dependencies and when the component unmounts.

cards.question: In production, when does a `useEffect` with an empty dependency array run?
cards.explanation: Empty deps means nothing can change, so it runs once after mount. In development, Strict Mode runs it twice to surface missing cleanup.

cards.question: Hooks may be called inside an `if` block as long as the condition rarely changes.
cards.explanation: React matches hooks by call order. Call them at the top level, in the same order every render, never conditionally.

cards.question: What does `useCallback(fn, deps)` return?
options: The same function until deps change
The cached result of calling fn
A function that runs only once
cards.explanation: useCallback keeps a function's identity stable, which helps memoized children and effect deps. useMemo caches a computed value instead.

cards.question: Leaving a used value out of a `useEffect` dependency array can make the effect read stale values.
cards.explanation: The effect keeps the values from the render it was created in. List every reactive value it reads; the exhaustive-deps lint rule catches misses.

cards.question: In package.json, which versions does `^1.4.2` allow?
cards.explanation: Caret ranges accept minor and patch updates below the next major. For 0.x versions the caret is stricter, since 0.x minors may break.

cards.question: `devDependencies` are for tools needed only to build or test, not at runtime.
cards.explanation: Compilers, bundlers, linters and test runners go there. Production installs such as `npm install --omit=dev` skip them.

cards.question: What does `"strict": true` in tsconfig.json enable?
options: A set of stricter checks like strictNullChecks
cards.explanation: `strict` turns on a family of compiler checks, including strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny. It adds no runtime checks.

cards.question: What does a lockfile such as package-lock.json provide?
options: The newest versions on every install
cards.explanation: The lockfile pins the full dependency tree. `npm ci` installs exactly what it lists, which keeps CI and teammates in sync.

cards.question: By default, esbuild and Vite type-check TypeScript and fail the build on type errors.
cards.explanation: They strip types without checking them, for speed. Run `tsc --noEmit` separately, for example in CI, to catch type errors.

cards.question: Who enforces CORS restrictions?
cards.explanation: The server sends CORS headers, but the browser decides whether the page's script may read the response.

cards.question: `fetch` rejects its promise when the server returns a 404 or 500.
cards.explanation: fetch rejects only on network failure. For HTTP errors it resolves; check `response.ok` or `response.status` yourself.

cards.question: How does `sessionStorage` differ from `localStorage`?
options: It's cleared when the tab's session ends
cards.explanation: sessionStorage is scoped to one tab and cleared when it closes. localStorage persists across tabs and restarts. Both store strings.

cards.question: CORS also blocks cross-origin requests made from Node.js or curl.
cards.explanation: CORS is a browser policy. Server-side code and curl ignore it, which is why a request can work in curl but fail in the browser.

cards.question: Which request triggers a CORS preflight OPTIONS request?
options: A cross-origin GET with no custom headers
A cross-origin POST with a JSON content type
cards.explanation: Requests beyond the 'simple' set, like a JSON Content-Type or custom headers, make the browser ask the server for permission first.
